name: Chunk-based spatial partitioning
text:
# Chunk-based spatial partitioning

Also called: Chunking, Block partitioning, Spatial decomposition

## Overview
Chunk-based spatial partitioning divides a volumetric dataset into fixed-size, contiguous spatial regions (chunks or blocks) to enable efficient memory management, parallel processing, and out-of-core streaming. It solves the problem of handling datasets larger than available RAM or single-processor capacity by allowing independent loading, rendering, or optimization of individual chunks. It differs from hierarchical methods like [Chunk Trees](4050-chunk-trees.md) by using a flat or uniform grid structure, and from view-dependent methods like [Sectioning](1636-sectioning.md) by maintaining a static spatial decomposition that is independent of the camera position.

## Shared principles
The family relies on decomposing the global domain $\Omega$ into a set of non-overlapping chunks $\{C_i\}$ such that $\Omega = \bigcup_i C_i$. Each chunk $C_i$ is associated with a fixed spatial extent, typically defined by axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs) in a [regular grid](#3950-regular-grid.md).

**Coordinate Mapping:**
For a uniform grid with chunk dimensions $W_x, W_y, W_z$, a global voxel coordinate $\mathbf{p} = (x, y, z)$ maps to a chunk index $\mathbf{k} = (k_x, k_y, k_z)$ and a local offset $\mathbf{p}_{local}$ via:
$$
k_x = \lfloor x / W_x \rfloor, \quad k_y = \lfloor y / W_y \rfloor, \quad k_z = \lfloor z / W_z \rfloor
$$
$$
\mathbf{p}_{local} = (x - k_x W_x, y - k_y W_y, z - k_z W_z)
$$
This mapping allows $O(1)$ determination of the chunk containing any sample point [Parent].

**Boundary Handling:**
Naive partitioning at chunk boundaries often introduces visual artifacts (e.g., black stripes in [compositing](#2436-compositing.md) or discontinuities in neural training) because rendering kernels or gradient calculations may span across chunk edges. To mitigate this, chunks often include an **overlap region** of width $w_{overlap}$. A chunk $C_i$ is extended to $C_i'$ such that it includes voxels from adjacent chunks $C_j$. During rendering or assembly, the overlapping data is either masked out or used to ensure continuity, while the final output is cropped to the original chunk boundaries [1093-mpi-based-volume-partitioning.md].

**I/O and Memory:**
Chunks are typically stored as independent files or memory blocks. This enables **streaming**, where only chunks within a certain distance of the camera or player are loaded into RAM, while others remain on disk [2369-chunk-based-world-streaming.md]. In distributed settings, chunks are assigned to specific nodes or processes, minimizing data movement during the core computation phase [1093-mpi-based-volume-partitioning.md].

## Subtopics

### [MPI-based Volume Partitioning](1093-mpi-based-volume-partitioning.md)
A data-parallel strategy where a volume is divided into contiguous slices along one axis (typically $z$) and assigned to distinct MPI processes. It minimizes inter-process communication during rendering by relying on post-processing assembly. It differs from streaming methods by processing a static snapshot and from training methods by focusing on visualization output. Key details include overlap handling to prevent boundary artifacts and optional mesh sewing for [isosurface extraction](#30-isosurface-extraction.md).

### [Chunk-based World Streaming](2369-chunk-based-world-streaming.md)
Divides a 3D voxel world into fixed-size spatial partitions (chunks) to manage memory and generation efficiently by loading only chunks near the player. It builds on spatial partitioning by managing chunk lifecycle, I/O scheduling, and state transitions (generation, meshing, unloading). It differs from static partitioning by dynamically loading/unloading chunks based on camera position and render distance.

### [Chunk-based Training](3168-chunk-based-training.md)
Optimizes neural volume representations on large-scale datasets by partitioning the global volume into fixed-size chunks, allowing independent optimization across multiple GPUs. It differs from single-GPU training by enabling parallel processing and from MPI-based partitioning by relying on independent chunk optimization rather than synchronized global gradient aggregation. It uses local coordinate spaces scaled to the global normalized volume.

### [Chunk Trees](4050-chunk-trees.md)
A planet-wide octree-based spatial partitioning method for voxel terrain rendering. It eliminates visible refinement artifacts and memory fragmentation by organizing data into a hierarchical structure of [chunk trees](#4050-chunk-trees.md). It differs from sibling methods by enforcing a screen-space cut that covers the entire world to prevent checker-hole artifacts, while using motion-aware detail levels to maintain performance during high-speed camera movement.

### [Object-space decomposition with local clustering](4156-object-space-decomposition-with-local-clustering.md)
A parallel volume rendering technique for unstructured grids that partitions the domain into view-independent clusters to minimize preprocessing overhead. Unlike uniform spatial partitioning, it groups neighboring cells into clusters of roughly equal computational weight using [graph partitioning](#4250-remapping-phase.md) (MeTiS). It serves as the static preprocessing foundation for the [Remapping Phase](4250-remapping-phase.md), which dynamically adjusts cluster assignments based on viewing parameters.

### [Uniform Block Partitioning with Acceleration](6098-uniform-block-partitioning-with-acceleration.md)
Divides a volume dataset into fixed-size spatial blocks to enable independent processing and applies [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md) techniques such as early ray termination, empty space skipping, and occlusion [clipping](#1444-clipping.md). It differs from streaming methods by focusing on static partitioning with immediate acceleration, and from Chunk Trees by using a flat uniform grid instead of a hierarchical tree structure.

### [Moving Walls Algorithm](9715-moving-walls-algorithm.md)
Partitions a volume dataset into cells containing closely cropped blocks of data, optimizing for a target memory size per cell. It solves the problem of distributing non-uniform, sparse volume data across a cluster by creating a view-independent partition that respects data boundaries, using dynamic programming to balance block sizes. It differs from standard uniform chunking by adapting cell boundaries to the geometry of the volume data (cropped slices) rather than a fixed grid.

#### VOGUE Parallel Operation
- **Step:** Divide dataset into subvolumes distributed across different units. Each unit processes a ray while it traverses its subvolume. On exit, send ray properties to the neighboring unit [S1].
- **Parameter:** Inter-unit communication uses a multi-master bus for up to 8 engines (640MB/s bandwidth) or a ring-connected cubic network for larger numbers (e.g., 4x4x4 units), requiring ~27MByte/s per link, total ~5.2GByte/s [S1].
- **Pitfall:** Gaps between subvolumes must be removed to avoid visual artifacts. This is done by replicating a certain set of boundary voxels [S1].

#### Efficient Query on Standard PCs
- **Definition:** An efficient data querying technique for large multivariate volume datasets, based on precomputed per-block Gaussian mixture models and run-time ellipse-polygon [intersection detection](#1705-voxel-filled-check.md), enabling interactive rendering on consumer-level PCs [S2, unofficial].
- **Step:** Precompute Gaussian mixture models per block of the volume data. Perform run-time ellipse-polygon intersection detection for data value querying [S2, unofficial].
- **Comparison:** Unlike hierarchical acceleration techniques like octrees which may not be beneficial for very dense multivariate data, this method uses precomputed models and geometric intersection for efficient querying [S2, unofficial].

## Background
Chunk-based partitioning is a fundamental technique in high-performance computing and graphics, originating from the need to handle datasets exceeding single-machine memory limits. Early architectures like COLOSSUS utilized subvolume distribution across parallel units to achieve speedups, introducing concepts like boundary voxel replication to maintain visual continuity [S1]. The method has since evolved to support out-of-core streaming for interactive applications (e.g., voxel games), distributed MPI rendering for scientific visualization, and parallel training of [neural radiance fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) (NeRFs) for large-scale scenes.
